Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Presenting problem: 6 days of dysuria with intermittent central lower abdominal (suprapubic) pain (reported severity 7/10), malodorous urine, and visible spotting of blood in urine. No fever, no flank/loin pain, no vaginal discharge. First episode.
- Clinician impression (from transcript): Most consistent with an acute uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis); treatment initiated empirically without urine testing.
- DDx support (consistent with transcript): 
  - Acute uncomplicated cystitis — high likelihood given dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine, visible hematuria.
  - Urethritis/STI — medium likelihood; can present with dysuria and urethral bleeding/spotting; sexual history limited.
  - Urolithiasis — medium likelihood; intermittent lower abdominal pain and hematuria can be caused by stones but lack of flank pain makes ureteric stone less typical.
  - Acute pyelonephritis/bladder cancer considered in DDx but less likely given lack of systemic features and risk factors; included in differential by diagnostic system but not favored clinically.
- Conflicts/limitations: No vital signs or urine testing to confirm diagnosis; antibiotic agent not named in the record (duration provided). No documented pregnancy status or complete sexual history. (See conflicts_summary below.)

Management Plan
- management_plan_main_or_not_recorded: 
  - Empiric antibiotic therapy prescribed; duration stated as 3 days. Antibiotic name, dose, route, frequency not documented.
  - Prescription sent to patient-requested pharmacy: Knightsbridge Practice; advised pick-up within ~1 hour (patient told ~lunchtime).
  - Advise increased oral fluids (recommended 2.5–3.0 L/day), cranberry juice as adjunct, and OTC sachets to alter urine acidity (details to be added to notes).
  - Advised to obtain a thermometer and check temperature at home.
  - Safety-netting: return or seek care if pain worsens, develops high temperature, develops flank/loin pain, has difficulty passing urine, or if symptoms are recurrent.
  - Follow-up: not required if symptoms resolve; reassess if not improving or recurrent.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute uncomplicated cystitis — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Female with 6 days of dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine and visible hematuria; no systemic features to suggest upper tract involvement. Supported by transcript and diagnostic reasoning.
- Urethritis (including STI) — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Dysuria with spotting can reflect urethritis; sexual history incompletely explored and patient denied recent intercourse, so consider if symptoms persist despite therapy.
- Urolithiasis (bladder/ureteric stone) — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Intermittent severe lower abdominal pain and hematuria can be caused by urinary stones; absence of flank pain and prior history makes this less classic but still plausible.
